claims.text: Wear performance in atmospheric-plasma-sprayed AlCoCrFeNi coatings is governed by the formation and distribution of nanoscale oxides.
Standard atmospheric plasma spraying of AlCoCrFeNi produces a characteristic nanoscale oxide dispersion.
Reducing oxygen availability during atmospheric plasma spraying reduces in-situ oxidation.
Reduced in-situ oxidation decreases the amount of nanoscale oxide inclusions in the coating.
Nanoscale oxides act as dispersion-strengthening features in AlCoCrFeNi coatings.
The nanoscale oxides refine the coating microstructure.
The nanoscale oxides obstruct dislocation motion.
The nanoscale oxides obstruct crack propagation.
Dispersion strengthening by nanoscale oxides increases coating hardness.
Increased hardness reduces material removal during sliding wear.
Coatings deposited at reduced oxygen partial pressure will have lower hardness than coatings deposited under standard atmospheric conditions.
Coatings deposited at reduced oxygen partial pressure will have higher wear rates than coatings deposited under standard atmospheric conditions.
The proposed relationship is expected to hold for atmospheric-plasma-sprayed AlCoCrFeNi coatings under moderate variations in oxygen level.
The proposed relationship may not extrapolate to extreme oxygen concentrations or different deposition methods.
Spray-condition variability may affect oxide formation independently of the imposed oxygen partial pressure.
The oxygen–oxide-content–wear relationship is not known quantitatively.
